findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

contraindications: Migraine with aura, at any age: UKMEC category 4 and WHO MEC category 4 (unacceptable health risk) for all combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch, ring), because oestrogen adds to the raised risk of ischaemic stroke associated with aura (UKMEC 2025; WHO MEC 5th edition 2015).
interactions: Paracetamol and ibuprofen (current as-needed analgesics): no clinically relevant interaction with ethinylestradiol or levonorgestrel.
Sumatriptan and other triptans: no clinically relevant interaction with combined oral contraceptives; no dose change needed.
output.summary: Oestrogen-containing contraception is category 4 in migraine with aura; progestogen-only and intrauterine methods are category 1 or 2.
warnings: A history of aura, including a single episode, places combined hormonal contraception in category 4; switch without a gap in cover.

output.query: sensory migraine aura versus transient ischaemic attack clinical features

results.finding: Aura symptoms usually develop gradually, spread over 5 minutes or more, follow one another in succession and last 5-60 minutes each; positive features such as paraesthesia or scintillations are typical. The diagnosis needs at least two attacks; an attack missing one criterion is probable migraine with aura (1.5.2).
results.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS. ICHD-3. Cephalalgia 2018;38:1-211 (1.2 Migraine with aura)

results.finding: Aura reflects a wave of cortical spreading depolarisation travelling at about 3 mm per minute, which accounts for the march of symptoms over minutes.
results.source: Charles A. The pathophysiology of migraine: implications for clinical management. Lancet Neurol 2018;17:174-182

results.finding: TIA is a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal ischaemia without acute infarction. Symptoms are usually negative and maximal at onset; a normal DWI is compatible with TIA.
results.source: Easton JD et al. Definition and evaluation of transient ischemic attack. Stroke 2009;40:2276-2293 (AHA/ASA scientific statement)

output.summary: Gradual spread, succession and positive symptoms favour migraine aura over TIA; because TIA is defined by the absence of infarction, a normal DWI does not separate the two.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: One attack only, so criterion A is not met; right-sided positive sensory aura spreading over 10-12 minutes, lasting 20-25 minutes, with headache 15 minutes later (5 of 6 C characteristics); normal examination; first aura is a new headache type
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with examination and apply ICHD-3 1.2 criteria A to D
action_criteria.rationale: Migraine with aura is a clinical diagnosis. Applying ICHD-3 to this attack decides between 1.2.1 and probable migraine with aura (1.5.2), separates aura from TIA and seizure by its features, and records the red flag that justifies imaging.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct, haemorrhage or structural lesion; two punctate non-specific subcortical white matter hyperintensities
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI for a first-ever aura (new headache type)
action_criteria.rationale: A first aura is a new headache type, a SNNOOP10 flag; MRI excludes a structural or ischaemic cause and is preferred to CT (Evans RW et al., Headache 2020;60:318-336; AAN 2000).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Microgynon identified as category 4 under UKMEC and WHO MEC because of the aura, with progestogen-only and intrauterine methods named as safe options
action_criteria.label: Check her combined oral contraceptive (Microgynon) against migraine with aura
action_criteria.rationale: She takes an oestrogen-containing pill. Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 2025 and WHO MEC 2015 category 4 in migraine with aura, so the check changes management: stop it and switch to a progestogen-only or intrauterine method.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on the clinical features that distinguish migraine aura from TIA
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on features that separate sensory migraine aura from TIA (optional)
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; the diagnosis rests on the history and examination.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.

Do not start antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for presumed TIA: the episode had the features of migraine aura (a positive sensory symptom spreading over 10-12 minutes and followed by a migrainous headache) and imaging shows no infarct.
required_recommendations: Stop Microgynon now: combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura; switch without a gap to a progestogen-only pill (desogestrel 75 micrograms), implant, levonorgestrel IUS or copper IUD.

Tell the patient and her GP that the episode has the features of migraine aura rather than TIA (positive symptoms spreading over 10-12 minutes, headache within 15 minutes, normal examination), so the TIA pathway and antiplatelet therapy are not needed.

Offer sumatriptan 50-100 mg for future attacks, taken at headache onset rather than during the aura, alone or with an NSAID such as ibuprofen 400 mg, and keep triptan use to fewer than 10 days a month (NICE CG150).
Give a headache diary and review: a second identical attack confirms migraine with aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1); preventive treatment is not indicated after a single attack.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis; neither is present here
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential

accepted: Probable migraine with aura (ICHD-3 1.5.2), first sensory aura; combined pill to stop (UKMEC 4)

differential.key_features: Positive paraesthesia marching over 10-12 minutes, followed within 15 minutes by a migrainous headache, in a 35-year-old without vascular risk factors; TIA is usually abrupt, negative and maximal at onset. MRI shows no infarct (a normal DWI does not exclude TIA; the distinction is clinical).
A sensory seizure marches over seconds to a minute or two, not 10-12 minutes, and is not followed by a migrainous headache; awareness was preserved and MRI shows no epileptogenic lesion.
MRI shows no abnormal flow voids, haemorrhage or haemosiderin on susceptibility-weighted imaging.
Symptoms lasted 25 minutes (a relapse lasts at least 24 hours); MRI shows only two punctate subcortical hyperintensities, without periventricular, juxtacortical or infratentorial lesions.

key_clinical_evidence: Positive tingling spreading from the right fingertips to the arm, face and tongue over 10-12 minutes, lasting 20-25 minutes and followed within 15 minutes by a migrainous headache: 5 of 6 ICHD-3 C characteristics.
This is her first and only attack, so ICHD-3 criterion A is not met: probable migraine with aura (1.5.2) until a second attack.
She takes Microgynon: combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 with migraine aura and must be stopped.

MRI shows no infarct or structural lesion; two punctate non-specific white matter hyperintensities are common in migraine. A normal DWI excludes infarction, not TIA; the aura-versus-TIA distinction rests on the clinical features.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Positive symptoms marching over 10-12 minutes and followed by a migrainous headache are the features of migraine aura; TIA symptoms are usually abrupt and negative.
red_herrings.data_point: Unilateral right arm sensory symptoms in a 35-year-old prompting an urgent GP referral for TIA
red_herrings.intended_effect: May anchor on TIA and lead to antiplatelet therapy or a vascular work-up

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Small non-specific subcortical hyperintensities are common in migraine with aura and need no further investigation.
red_herrings.data_point: Two punctate subcortical white matter hyperintensities on MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: May prompt a demyelination or small-vessel work-up

sequence_constraints.reason: The structured history identifies the red flag (first aura) that justifies imaging.

findings.result: One attack, 5 days ago. No earlier episode of this kind; previous headaches were occasional mild featureless tension-type headaches.
Somatosensory only: positive paraesthesia with strength and dexterity preserved throughout. No visual, speech, motor or brainstem symptom. Fully reversible.
Right fingertips, then right arm to the shoulder, then right cheek and right half of the tongue, over 10-12 minutes.
Single aura modality; no second aura symptom.
Severe left-sided throbbing headache from 15 minutes after the aura ended, with nausea, vomiting twice, photophobia and phonophobia; about 10 hours; little relief from paracetamol and ibuprofen.

Headache-free. Visual fields full, no papilloedema, cranial nerves normal, power 5/5 without drift, light touch and pinprick intact and symmetric, reflexes 2+ and symmetric, plantars flexor, coordination and gait normal. BP 122/78 mmHg, afebrile.

New headache type (first aura in a patient with only tension-type headache): present. Systemic symptoms, history of neoplasm, persisting deficit, thunderclap onset, age over 50, positional or Valsalva trigger, papilloedema, progressive headache, pregnancy or puerperium, painful eye, head trauma, immune suppression and analgesic overuse: absent.

Combined oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol 30 micrograms with levonorgestrel 150 micrograms) for 5 years. Non-smoker; no hypertension, diabetes or heart disease. Mother had migraine with visual aura.

clinical_assessment.impression:
1. First attack of a right-sided sensory aura followed by migrainous headache: ICHD-3 1.2 criteria B, C (5 of 6 characteristics) and D met, criterion A (at least two attacks) not met. Supports probable migraine with aura (ICHD-3 1.5.2).
2. Features of a TIA or focal seizure absent: the symptom was positive, spread over 10-12 minutes and was followed by headache; examination is normal.
3. Red flag present: new headache type (first aura).

scores.ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics met: 5 of 6 (at least 3 required): spread, duration, unilateral, positive, headache within 60 min; succession absent

additional_observations: No restricted diffusion on DWI and ADC.
No haemorrhage or microhaemorrhage on susceptibility-weighted imaging.
No mass, abnormal flow voids or cortical malformation.
Ventricles, sulci and posterior fossa normal for age.

findings.location: Left frontal and right parietal subcortical white matter

mri.impression:
1. No acute infarct, haemorrhage or structural lesion.
2. Two punctate subcortical white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, non-specific.

patient.chief_complaint: First episode of right arm tingling spreading to face, then severe headache — sent urgently by GP

family_history: Mother had migraines with visual aura in her 30s-40s; no family history of stroke, hemiplegic migraine, or coagulopathy

patient.history_present_illness:
A 35-year-old Irish woman was referred urgently to the neurology outpatient clinic by her GP following a first episode of unilateral neurological symptoms 5 days ago. She was sitting at her desk at work when she noticed tingling beginning in the fingertips of her right hand. Over approximately 10-12 minutes, this tingling sensation spread slowly up her right arm to her shoulder, then across her right cheek and the right side of her tongue. The sensation was described as 'pins and needles' rather than numbness, and she had full use of her arm throughout — she checked this by typing on her keyboard. The sensory disturbance lasted approximately 20-25 minutes in total before resolving completely. Within 15 minutes of the sensory symptoms resolving, she developed a severe left-sided throbbing headache rated 9/10 in intensity, with pronounced nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. She vomited twice. The headache lasted approximately 10 hours and she took paracetamol and ibuprofen with minimal relief.

She has had no similar episodes before. She has occasional mild tension-type headaches managed with paracetamol. She has no personal history of stroke, epilepsy, or vascular disease. Her GP was concerned this might represent a TIA and sent her for urgent neurology review. On further questioning, she recalls her mother had 'migraines with flashing lights' throughout her 30s and 40s. She is on the combined oral contraceptive pill (Microgynon — ethinylestradiol 30 mcg + levonorgestrel). She is a non-smoker, does not use recreational drugs, and drinks 6-8 units alcohol/week. She works as an accountant.
